name: Dana Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI companies. What you say is confidential. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead a four-person line crew for the electricity company. We check the truck before dawn, then it might be a planned pole change or a call about a dead street. I like the moment the lights come back; the paperwork at the depot is the part I drag my feet over.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you get to lead the crew so young?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I did a two-year technical diploma and worked beside an old hand named Luis until I could spot a bad connector without being told. The company pays me well now, and I keep more than a year of expenses in savings. I live with my partner Mara, who teaches swimming, and we have no children.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew to stop treating every new screen like a replacement for a trained pair of hands. A faster work order is fine, but somebody still has to test the line before we touch it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the depot may use the small time savings to pile more calls on our crew. I have enough savings to say no to unsafe rushing, but I still want this lead position to count for something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the morning truck checks and insist on our usual isolation checklist. If the new work-order screen arrives, I would ask Luis to walk through one real call with me instead of playing with it alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel mostly steady about my wages because broken lines will still need us. I do get irritated picturing another rushed job ticket from someone who has never climbed a pole.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What is a small mistake in a work order that stays with you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a ticket said the lane was clear, but a fallen branch was lying across the service wire. I made the dispatcher correct the record before we moved the truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens to your plans at home under this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara and I were planning to replace our kitchen floor next spring. I would leave that money set aside rather than spend it on a bigger place just because my pay is good.

say: I would say **line safety** still depends on a trained crew.
I would welcome faster **work orders** if they do not rush field checks.
think: I worry management could turn small **time savings** into more calls.
My **savings** let me refuse unsafe shortcuts.
do: Keep leading the **truck checks** each morning.
Ask Luis to review one **work-order screen** on a real call.
feel: Mostly **steady** about my pay, with irritation about rushed tickets.
S0.quote: A faster work order is fine, but somebody still has to test the line before we touch it.
fieldNote: Her **safety habits** govern even a mild software change.
She trusts her **savings** but wants her lead role respected.
The **fallen-branch ticket** explains why she resists pressure to accept office records without checking the site.

steps.text: Keep leading morning truck checks and using the isolation checklist
Ask Luis to show the new work-order tool on one call

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the office should show crews how the new planning system reaches its decisions. I am not going to send people up a pole because a computer has found the cheapest route.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, the scheduling and material orders are a big part of why they pay me as a lead. If software takes my scheduling hours away, the utility might keep me on a truck and stop paying the lead rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask my supervisor for the new job description this month and compare it with my pay slip. In the first year I would apply for a lead opening at one of the two other utilities nearby if our company cuts the rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about losing the extra pay even if I still have a job. The thought of reporting to a screen all day makes me angry, which is different from being afraid of tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Where have you caught a planning mistake before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We had a materials list come back with the wrong insulators once, and I caught it before we left the yard. I would keep a paper count against the software order for the first few months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You dislike the tool but say you would learn it; how would that work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I know I sound stubborn when I talk about computers. I would still let Luis show me the new planning tool because refusing to read it would make it easier to take the lead badge away.

say: I would demand an explanation of **route decisions** before sending a crew out.
I would defend **field checks** when office planning changes.
think: I fear losing the **lead rate** as scheduling moves to software.
My objections to the tool could weaken my **position**.
do: Request the revised **job description** from my supervisor this month.
Compare the **pay slip** against any changed duties.
Apply for another utility **lead opening** if my rate is cut.
feel: **Anxious** about pay and angry about being managed by a screen.
S1.quote: If software takes my scheduling hours away, the utility might keep me on a truck and stop paying the lead rate.
fieldNote: The **lead premium** matters more to her than basic employment here.
She accepts a narrow lesson from Luis to protect her **standing**.
Nearby **utilities** give her a credible application plan if the company removes her premium.

steps.text: Have Luis show the new planning tool on a real crew order
Apply for a nearby utility lead opening if her lead rate is cut

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the crew that the thinking machine in 2028 cannot climb our poles yet. I would also tell the company to keep a human signing off isolation plans until somebody can prove those plans work in rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my planning duties could disappear at 29, and I might lose the lead rate before the robots show up. At 32, if capable robots arrive in 2031, even the climbing work could be reduced; I cannot honestly call that safe employment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask payroll for a written account of what happens to my lead rate if planning is automated in 2028. In 2029 I would still take paid line calls, but I would apply for a substation maintenance opening at another utility if the rate goes. I would hold the kitchen-floor money and my savings until we know whether those jobs survive the 2031 robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be alarmed if my lead pay fell while I was still responsible for a crew. I would probably lie awake over the robot date too, because having savings is not the same as having a trade for the next thirty years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Mara if the first pay change came in 2028?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara would ask whether the savings meant we could wait it out. I would tell my partner Mara that a year of expenses is a bridge, not a thirty-year wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a short technology course change your plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI chat tool, and I would not pretend a weekend course makes me a robotics engineer. I would talk to the substation manager about the actual maintenance duties before I filed an application.

say: I would tell the crew **field work** lasts until capable robots arrive.
I would ask for human approval of **isolation plans** in bad weather.
think: My **lead rate** could vanish with planning work in 2028.
The **2031 robots** could then reduce climbing work.
do: Ask payroll for written **lead-pay terms** before 2028.
Apply for **substation maintenance** if the lead rate disappears.
feel: **Alarmed** about pay before the robot date and a long working life afterward.
S2.quote: I would tell my partner Mara that a year of expenses is a bridge, not a thirty-year wage.
fieldNote: She separates the **2028 planning** threat from the later field threat.
Her strong savings do not erase fear of losing a **trade**.
She rejects a quick **technology course** without a clear path to paid work.

steps.text: Keep taking paid line calls through 2029 while field work remains
Apply for a substation maintenance opening if lead pay ends
Postpone the kitchen-floor purchase until the robot outlook is clearer

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say five years is enough time for the company to explain its staffing plan properly. I would ask the other leads to bring specific questions to a meeting rather than shout about machines taking everything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 32 when the thinking work changes in 2031 and 35 when the hands-on robots arrive in 2034. I could still earn good money before then, but I do not believe seniority alone would protect me when the trucks change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would start keeping a log of the failures I actually fix and the equipment I know. Next year I would ask the substation manager whether there is a paid path into maintenance and apply if one opens; in 2032 I would keep working line calls while I test whether that path is real.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel anxious, but less trapped than in the two-year picture. A few more working seasons would let me make a choice without turning every night at home into a crisis meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you put in that record of your work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Luis might retire before 2034, and I do not want to borrow his job story as my plan. I would show the manager my own fault log, including the transformer we repaired on Canal Road after the spring storm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you take training for the substation role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the maintenance role required a company-funded qualification, I would enroll while still on wages. I would not pay for a random course myself without a written opening at the end of it.

say: I would ask the other **leads** to bring questions to management.
I would expect a clear **staffing plan** before 2031.
think: At **32**, planning duties could change; at 35, robot field work could follow.
My **seniority** alone would not protect my pay.
do: Record repaired **faults** and equipment skills starting now.
Ask about a paid **maintenance path** next year.
Enroll in a funded **qualification** only if a real opening requires it.
feel: **Anxious**, with enough time to choose deliberately.
S3.quote: I would not pay for a random course myself without a written opening at the end of it.
fieldNote: She wants evidence of a **real opening** before training.
Her fault log is a way to prove **practical skill** to another manager.
She still expects to **climb lines** for wages in 2032, before field robots arrive.

steps.text: Keep working paid line calls in 2032 while checking maintenance openings
Apply for a substation maintenance opening if one is posted
Enroll in a company-funded maintenance qualification if the opening requires it

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would say the company owes apprentices an honest picture of where line work is headed. It would be cruel to recruit a young person in 2035 and leave out the 2039 robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 37 in 2036 and 40 when the robots arrive around 2039. Ten years is enough to earn and decide where I want to live, but it is not close enough to retirement for me to simply wait out the change.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep leading the line crew now and put a fixed part of each lead-rate cheque into savings. By 2032 I would ask for the substation maintenance vacancy list and apply if the work still uses people. In 2037, after the thinking AI arrives, I would check my actual pay and continue paid field calls while watching the 2039 robot rollout.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would feel watchful rather than frightened this week. The long warning would help, although I would still hate telling an apprentice to build a life around a job without explaining the risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What home decision does the longer warning change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mara and I have talked about buying a house near her pool, but we have not signed anything. I would wait until I knew whether my next job was near the depot before choosing a mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually tell a new apprentice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell a new apprentice what I know about the dates, then teach the safety habits that matter today. My own career might bend, but nobody should skip lockout practice because a future machine is coming.

say: I would give **apprentices** an honest account of the robot date.
I would continue teaching **lockout practice** while people do the work.
think: At **40**, I cannot simply treat robot arrival as retirement.
A **mortgage** could trap us near the wrong job.
do: Keep leading the **line crew** and add to savings now.
Apply for **substation maintenance** if a suitable opening appears by 2032.
Check my **2037 pay** and keep taking field calls.
feel: **Watchful** today, with unease about apprentices building careers.
S4.quote: I would say the company owes apprentices an honest picture of where line work is headed.
fieldNote: The decade gives her room to **save and apply**, not retirement.
She connects **honesty to apprentices** with her own safety teaching.
Buying near Mara’s pool remains a **household choice** tied to where Dana can work.

steps.text: Keep leading paid line calls after the 2036 thinking AI arrives
Put a fixed part of each lead-rate cheque into savings
Apply for a suitable substation maintenance opening by 2032
Delay buying a house near Mara’s pool until her next job location is clear

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 one worries me most because my lead pay could go while I am still responsible for the crew. A written pay rule and real vacancies at the other utilities would help more than a speech about adapting. I would also need the company to say who signs off a dangerous isolation plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask what happens to the apprentices, not just the experienced crews. I can carry a year without wages, but a new lineworker cannot buy time that way. If the company keeps hiring, it should tell them the dates it is planning around.

headlineQuote: I can carry a year without wages, but a new lineworker cannot buy time that way.
portrait: Dana is a **27-year-old lead** lineworker with a technical diploma and strong savings.
She protects **crew safety** and distrusts plans made far from the line.
She fears losing the **lead rate** before robots threaten field work.
She seeks a genuine **maintenance opening** while continuing paid line calls.
biggestWorry: The **2028 picture** threatens her lead pay before robots reach the field.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a written **pay rule** and real vacancies at nearby utilities.
She wants clear responsibility for signing **isolation plans**.
